title: Keystroke tracking for remote claims adjusters
scenario: Beatriz Almeida directs operations at a Lisbon insurance back office whose adjusters have worked from home since the pandemic. Productivity dipped slightly, and her chief executive wants keystroke and mouse-activity tracking with automatic flags for idle stretches. Beatriz knows several adjusters care for children or ill parents and work in irregular bursts, yet deliver accurate claims. A union representative has asked her to resist. The board will review remote-work policy on Friday, and Beatriz must tell them whether her department can justify exemption from the monitoring programme.
options: Accept the tracking but ask for a pilot with team-level reporting only, so individuals are not scored on idle time.
Argue for exemption, offering outcome targets such as claims closed and error rates in place of activity tracking.
Support full tracking as proposed, trusting that data will protect hardworking staff from unfair suspicion and make decisions more objective.

title: Thermal cameras on the factory floor
scenario: At a garment factory outside Dhaka, plant manager Rubel Hossain has been offered thermal cameras that detect fever and also record how long each worker spends away from machines. Buyers abroad demand better safety audits after a recent respiratory outbreak, and the cameras would help keep the line open. Workers fear the break-time data will be used to dock wages, and the supplier's contract does not forbid it. Rubel must sign the purchase by the end of the week or lose an order from a large overseas retailer that could employ two thousand people.
options: Buy the cameras with fever detection only, disabling break-time logging in writing and inviting worker representatives to verify it.
Decline the purchase and use manual temperature checks, accepting the risk of losing the retailer's contract and jobs.
Buy the full system and promise informally that break-time data will not be used for wages, relying on goodwill to maintain trust.

title: Reading a nurse's wearable badge data
scenario: Hospital administrator Dr. Margit Szabo in Budapest learns that location badges, introduced to speed emergency response, can show how long each nurse spends at a patient's bedside. After a patient death on a night shift, the family's lawyer demands the badge records, and the hospital's own review board wants to use them to judge the nurses involved. Nurses were told the badges were for safety only. Margit knows the data might reveal understaffing rather than negligence, but it could also expose an individual nurse to blame. A response is due to the lawyer in forty-eight hours.
options: Release the badge data as requested, since the family deserves a full account and the data may show systemic understaffing.
Withhold the data on the grounds of the original purpose limit, offering the family a summary report and independent review instead.
Use the data internally for the board review but anonymise individual nurses in anything shared outside the hospital.
tension: truth for the bereaved vs. promises to staff

title: Cameras in the cab of a long-haul truck
scenario: Haruna Bello owns a small trucking firm in northern Nigeria with eleven drivers. After a fatal crash involving a competitor, his insurer offered a discount if he installs driver-facing cameras that detect drowsiness and phone use. His drivers, many with decades of experience, feel insulted and worry about being watched in the cab, where they pray, eat and sometimes speak to family. The discount would save Haruna a significant share of his annual premium, and he suspects a drowsy-driving risk is real on overnight routes. He has to sign by month end or lose the offer.
options: Install the cameras with drowsiness alerts only and no stored footage, accepting a lesser insurance discount if the insurer permits.
Install the full camera system and keep footage, arguing safety for the public and the drivers themselves outweighs discomfort.
Decline the cameras and use rest-hour limits, honest check-ins and a bonus for incident-free months, accepting the higher premium.

title: A school bus app that tracks teenagers
scenario: Councillor Siobhan Gallagher chairs a rural Irish school transport committee considering an app that gives parents real-time GPS location of children on buses and records when each pupil boards. Parents of younger pupils strongly want it after a child was left at the wrong stop. Older pupils, aged fifteen to seventeen, object that this tracks their movements and could reveal when they skip classes or visit relatives parents disapprove of. The app vendor sells the same product for all ages. Siobhan must put a motion to the committee on Thursday evening.
options: Adopt the app for all pupils, since a single policy is simpler and child safety concerns outweigh the older students' objections.
Adopt it only for primary-age pupils, leaving teenagers to an opt-in arrangement they can control themselves.
Reject the app and fund extra bus supervisors, accepting a higher cost per pupil and fewer real-time safeguards.

title: Emotion detection in a Shenzhen sales office
scenario: Wei Lan, head of people analytics at a Chinese electronics retailer, has been shown software that analyses the facial expressions of sales staff during customer calls and scores their friendliness. Her executive team believes it will raise sales, and pilot sites improved by five percent. Wei has read that such emotion inference is unreliable across individuals and cultures, and some employees say forced smiling is exhausting. Several staff in the pilot resigned. A company-wide rollout needs her recommendation, due in a week, and her own bonus depends on analytics adoption.
options: Recommend rollout with scores used only for coaching and never for pay or dismissal decisions, accepting that this is hard to enforce.
Recommend against rollout, citing unreliable science and staff burnout, even though pilot sales rose and executives want it.
Recommend an opt-in version for volunteers, with transparent reporting of resulting sales outcomes before any wider decision.

title: Monitoring a lone worker on an oil platform
scenario: Safety officer Ingvar Solheim oversees a North Sea platform where a wrist device tracks the heart rate and location of crew members to detect emergencies. After a fall that went unnoticed for forty minutes, management wants the data kept and analysed to predict fatigue, which would also reveal underlying conditions such as heart irregularities or stress. Crew members are not sure what happens to those findings, and fear losing their certification. Ingvar can design the retention policy, but his employer, not a doctor, will own the data.
options: Keep only real-time emergency data and delete it daily, giving up fatigue prediction to protect crew medical privacy.
Retain data for fatigue analysis, but store it with an independent occupational health provider that releases only fit-for-duty determinations.
Retain and analyse all data in-house, telling crew clearly what is collected, because safety on a remote platform justifies broader use.

title: The union rep and the badge swipe logs
scenario: Lerato Mokoena works as an IT systems administrator for a mining company in South Africa. A supervisor quietly asks her to pull door-access logs showing which employees attended an unauthorised meeting the previous night. She suspects it was a union planning session ahead of a wage dispute, though the supervisor says it is about a theft. She has legitimate technical access, and refusing might make her the target of suspicion. The theft is genuine and affected several teams. The supervisor wants the list by close of business today.
options: Provide the logs for the specific time window of the theft only, with no names related to the meeting, and record the request in writing.
Refuse to run the query without written authorisation from HR or legal, accepting the supervisor's displeasure.
Provide the full list as requested, since it is lawful company data and the theft needs investigating.
tension: employer instruction vs. workers' right to organise

title: Working-from-home screenshots for a freelance translator
scenario: Yui Nakagawa runs a Tokyo translation agency using a platform that requires freelancers to allow random screenshots every ten minutes to prove hours worked on hourly contracts. A longtime freelancer, a medical interpreter, tells Yui the screenshots capture confidential patient records she translates and her private messages. The client is a hospital group that insists on proof of hours. Dropping the platform means switching to a rival with weaker protections or negotiating per-word payment, which the hospital may reject. Yui must tell the freelancer something by tomorrow, as an assignment is waiting.
options: Offer the freelancer a per-word rate without screenshots, and ask the hospital to accept it, risking the contract.
Keep the screenshot requirement but blur sensitive windows through software, accepting that blurring may fail.
Assign the medical work to a different freelancer who is comfortable with the screenshots, protecting the contract but denying her work.

title: Cafe cameras that count staff chat
scenario: Owner Dimitra Papadaki runs three seaside cafes in Crete and has been trialling a camera system that tracks queue times. The vendor's update can also measure how long employees chat with each other and flags it as idle. Dimitra is aware that tourists are impatient and that two staff members previously spent too long socialising. The same staff are the reason many regular customers return. Her margins are thin in the off season. She needs to decide whether to enable the new feature before the busy summer begins next week.
options: Enable the feature and share the weekly reports openly with staff, treating it as a shared tool for improving service.
Leave the feature disabled and address chatting through direct conversation with the two staff concerned.
Enable it for a month with staff agreement, then review together whether it actually improved service or just stress.

title: Predicting which employees will resign
scenario: Anand Deshpande, an HR data scientist at a Bangalore software services firm, has built a model that predicts which employees are likely to resign from email patterns, badge-ins and calendar changes. Managers want to use it to offer retention bonuses, but some also hint they might skip training investment for people flagged as flight risks. Anand knows employees were never told these signals feed into a prediction. The model is accurate, and the company is losing talent fast. He is due to present it to the leadership team on Wednesday and must decide how to frame its permitted use.
options: Present it with a strict rule that it may only trigger supportive conversations and retention offers, never adverse decisions.
Hold back the model until employees have been told and have consented to this use of their work data, delaying retention efforts.
Present the model as is and leave decisions about its use to managers, who understand their teams better than he does.

title: Teachers monitored by classroom microphones
scenario: Headteacher Kwame Asante in Kumasi has been offered free classroom audio devices by a donor that transcribe lessons and score teacher talk time and student participation. The donor's goal is better teaching quality and data for a national study. Kwame's teachers fear the recordings could be used against them, as classroom discussions sometimes touch on politically sensitive or religious topics. Student voices would also be captured. The school is under-resourced, and the devices come with free training and a stipend. The donor wants an answer before the term begins in ten days.
options: Accept the devices with a written agreement that transcripts stay on-site, are deleted weekly, and are used only for teachers' own self-review.
Decline the donation and look for other training support, protecting teachers and students at the cost of resources the school badly needs.
Accept the full programme including data sharing for the national study, judging the long-term benefit to Ghanaian education as outweighing the risks.

title: Driver behaviour scores at a Bogota bus company
scenario: Fleet supervisor Camilo Restrepo's company installed sensors that score bus drivers on harsh braking and acceleration. A driver, Doña Marta, a widow with twenty years of service, keeps receiving low scores because she drives the steepest route and regularly brakes hard to avoid cyclists and street vendors who step into the road. Under the rules, three low months mean a pay penalty. Camilo knows the scoring does not adjust for route difficulty. Reprogramming the scoring needs the vendor and could take months. Pay decisions are made at the end of this week.
options: Apply the penalty according to policy, since a fair system treats everyone by the same published rules.
Waive the penalty for Marta and ask the vendor to adjust for route difficulty, accepting that other drivers may demand equal treatment.
Suspend all pay penalties for every driver on difficult routes until the scoring is corrected, accepting added safety risk elsewhere.

title: Smart office desks and the pregnant engineer
scenario: Facilities manager Johanna Eriksson at a Finnish engineering firm learned that the new smart-desk sensors, installed to optimise space, record how often individual employees leave their desks. A pregnant engineer, Aino, who needs frequent breaks, has been flagged in a space-utilisation report that managers see by name. Aino has not told her team about her pregnancy. The vendor can anonymise the report, but doing so removes the ability to catch genuine desk-hoarding that the company has complained about. Johanna must send the monthly report to department heads tomorrow morning.
options: Anonymise the report immediately for everyone, giving up the ability to identify desk-hoarding by name.
Send the named report but quietly remove Aino's entry, without telling her, to protect her without changing policy for others.
Send the report as is, since it reflects policy applied to everyone, and let Aino raise any accommodation needs through HR.

title: Informal lending circle on a monitored work network
scenario: Systems security analyst Olumide Adeyemi in Lagos notices through network monitoring that a group of warehouse employees runs a rotating savings circle through a workplace chat app, which is against the acceptable use policy. The circle quietly helps low-paid workers cover emergencies, and several of them would be unable to access formal credit. His supervisor asked for monthly reports on policy violations. Olumide knows reporting it will lead to warnings or dismissals, while hiding it would breach his duty and might expose him if audited. The next report is due Monday.
options: Report the activity accurately as the policy requires, and propose that the company create a sanctioned alternative savings scheme.
Leave it out of the report and warn the workers informally to move their activity off the network.
Report only aggregate numbers without names, and recommend a policy review rather than individual discipline.

title: Facial login for night-shift hospital cleaners
scenario: Contract manager Esperanza Rojas in Manila supplies cleaning staff to a private hospital that now requires face-scan clock-ins. Some of her cleaners, who are Muslim women wearing a niqab, cannot comfortably use the system, and the fallback fingerprint reader repeatedly fails on workers whose fingerprints are worn from chemical cleaning agents. The hospital says manual sign-in invites time fraud, which it has experienced. Esperanza risks losing the contract if the hospital considers her compliance poor. The hospital's facilities head has asked for a decision on how her team will clock in by next payroll cycle.
options: Ask the hospital to allow supervisor-verified paper sign-in for affected workers, accepting its fraud concerns and the contract risk.
Require all workers to use the face scan, offering private rooms where women can uncover briefly, to preserve the contract.
Replace affected workers with others who can use the system easily, protecting the contract but removing experienced staff.

title: A union steward found through productivity data
scenario: Data analyst Mateusz Kowalczyk-Reyes at a Spanish call centre is asked by the director to identify employees whose call volumes dropped sharply on the days before a strike vote, supposedly to plan staffing. Mateusz realises the analysis would effectively identify supporters of the strike. He is on a temporary contract that is up for renewal in a month. Refusing might jeopardise his job, and he could simply provide the numbers and say he did not interpret them. The director expects the dataset by the end of the day.
options: Provide the data as requested, taking no part in how it is later used, since the numbers are neutral and the decision belongs to management.
Decline to produce it and explain in writing that it may breach workers' rights, accepting the risk to his renewal.
Provide aggregated data only at team level, which meets the stated staffing purpose but cannot identify individuals.

title: Voice analytics on a crisis hotline
scenario: Pastor-turned-manager Elijah Njoroge runs a suicide-prevention hotline in Uganda staffed by volunteers. A donor offers software that analyses calls for volunteer tone and flags those who sound disengaged, promising better quality control. Volunteers are unpaid, many are survivors of crisis themselves, and some say being scored would drain their motivation. The recordings would also contain intimate details of callers who were promised confidentiality. Donor funding makes up half the budget. Elijah has to answer the donor before the end of the financial year, which is next week.
options: Decline the software and keep confidential, peer-supported quality review among volunteers, accepting the loss of half the funding to protect callers.
Accept it with call content deleted immediately and only tone metrics retained, telling callers and volunteers clearly beforehand.
Accept the software fully to preserve funding for the hotline, reasoning that keeping the service open helps more callers than strict privacy would.

title: Employee wellness app with a trackable step count
scenario: Wellness programme lead Camille Beaulieu at a Quebec manufacturing company launched a voluntary step-count app that gives discounts on health insurance. Participation reached seventy percent. She now learns that the vendor can supply the employer with individual-level data, and the finance director wants to use it to identify employees with low activity for targeted health coaching, which sounds helpful, but may lead to quiet pressure. Employees who opted out say they feel subtly penalised. Camille must decide this month what data the company may receive and use.
options: Receive only aggregated, anonymous data and use it for general programmes, ending individual-level coaching referrals.
Allow targeted coaching offers to low-activity participants who have specifically opted in to receive them.
Accept the full individual data and run targeted outreach, because early intervention could help employees avoid serious illness.

title: Cameras at the Sydney aged-care facility
scenario: Director of nursing Bronwyn Tran manages an aged-care home where a family has demanded cameras in their mother's room after finding bruises. Staff say cameras would violate their dignity and that of other residents who share nearby corridors, and the union objects to constant observation of care workers. Bruising might be due to rough handling or simply fragile skin. The mother has dementia and cannot say whether she consents. Bronwyn must decide whether to allow the camera before the family's lawyer sends a formal complaint on Monday.
options: Allow the camera inside the room only, with visible signage, staff notification and strict limits on who can view footage.
Refuse the camera and offer independent clinical examination plus increased staff documentation of care, protecting all residents' and staff's dignity.
Allow the camera and also extend monitoring to all residents' rooms where families request it, treating cameras as a consistent safety measure.
tension: protecting a vulnerable resident vs. staff dignity

title: Scanning a politician's driver's phone
scenario: Chief of security Dragan Petrovic at a Serbian ministry learns that staff phones are managed by software that can read messages. The minister's driver, a long-serving employee, is suspected by an anonymous tip of passing details of the minister's schedule to journalists. Reading the messages is technically possible and arguably allowed by his contract, though the driver might also be exchanging private messages about his sick child. The minister's office wants an answer within hours before an important summit. Dragan must decide on a course of action without time for legal advice.
options: Search the driver's messages narrowly for contact with named journalists and nothing else, then report only that finding.
Do not read any messages, reassign the driver temporarily and raise the concern through a formal, lawful investigation.
Read the full contents of the driver's phone to resolve the matter quickly and guarantee the minister's safety at the summit.

title: Gig couriers and the fraud-detection location check
scenario: Operations lead Tuan Nguyen at a Ho Chi Minh City delivery app uses GPS checks to detect couriers faking their location to claim orders. The fraud costs the company real money and takes work from honest couriers. However, the checks also suspend couriers whose phones lose signal in dense high-rise areas, and appeals take days during which they earn nothing. Tuan can loosen the rules, which would reduce false suspensions but let more fraud through, or keep them tight. Several couriers have gathered outside the office and local media attention is increasing.
options: Loosen the check and instead recover fraud losses through post-hoc audits, accepting more fraud for fewer wrongful suspensions.
Keep the strict check and add a same-day appeals desk, accepting the cost and some continuing wrongful suspensions.
Keep the check unchanged and pay a small allowance for couriers suspended wrongly, compensating but not removing the problem.

title: A shared-flat smart lock and domestic workers
scenario: Property manager Nasrin Tehrani in Toronto is considering smart locks for a building where many tenants employ live-in domestic workers. The locks log every entry and exit, and the app is owned by the tenant, so employers can see when their workers come and go, on days off as well. Some tenants say this helps protect them from theft. Workers' advocates warn it enables control of people who may already be isolated. Nasrin cannot restrict how tenants use their own access logs without breaking the standard service terms. The contract must be signed at the end of the week.
options: Sign the contract but negotiate an option for each person to see their own logs and bar logs from being shared with others without consent.
Choose a different lock system that does not retain entry logs, accepting higher cost and reduced security for tenants.
Sign as offered, since tenant privacy and property rights belong to the tenants, and leave the question of domestic workers to labour law.
tension: tenant rights vs. vulnerable third parties

title: Reading a fisherman's tracker after a rival's accusation
scenario: Cooperative secretary Tevita Fifita in Tonga oversees satellite trackers that boats must carry to prove they stay outside a protected reef. A rival captain accuses a fellow fisherman, Sione, of entering the reserve, and demands the tracker data be shown at the village meeting tonight. The data are held by the cooperative and Sione, who has fed half the village during hard seasons, says the tracker malfunctioned. Publicly airing the data could shame him even if the error was real. Tevita holds the only login, and the rules do not specify who may see individual boat data.
options: Show the data privately to a small panel of elders and Sione together, and report only their conclusion to the meeting.
Display the data at the meeting as the rival requests, treating transparency as essential to protecting the reef the whole village relies on.
Refuse to release anything until the cooperative formally writes a rule on data access, delaying resolution beyond the meeting.

title: Eye-tracking exams for remote medical students
scenario: Dean Valeria Contreras-Okafor at a distance-learning medical school in Argentina uses proctoring software that tracks eye movements and flags students who look away from the screen. Students with ADHD, vision conditions, or cramped shared homes are flagged far more often, and several have been accused of cheating on that basis alone. Cheating did rise before the software was introduced, and graduates will treat real patients. Appeals are heard by a panel that meets monthly. Final exams start in nine days, and Valeria must set the rules for how flags will be treated.
options: Treat flags only as prompts for a human to review the recording, never as grounds for sanction without further evidence.
Keep the current automatic sanction process, since the integrity of medical qualifications protects future patients.
Replace remote proctoring with supervised in-person exams at regional centres, accepting travel burdens for students in distant provinces.
tension: exam integrity vs. fair treatment of disabled students
